paras: The lynching of "Nosey" Smith was the hanging of a man by vigilantes at Sun River, Montana Territory, reported in January 1888. According to a dispatch from Macleod in the Northwest Territories, he was accused of having shamefully abused his two daughters and was hanged after returning to Montana to get them back. The brief item ran in papers from Virginia to Oregon, and a year-end tally later counted him among the year's victims of "Judge Lynch."

Smith was described as well known around Macleod, where he had arrived from Montana about two years earlier "in rather hurried manner." He told people there he had left to escape "the persecution of his enemies," but reports from Montana said he had fled to avoid being hanged for abusing his daughters. While in Macleod he claimed that two of his daughters were being kept in a convent near Sun River against his wishes and theirs; the dispatch said the girls had been placed there "for their own safety" because he habitually abused them.

The Macleod dispatch said that "last month" Smith crossed the border into Montana, tried to take the girls, and gave a priest "a severe pummeling." Vigilantes then seized him and shut him in a building. They told him they would release him if he confessed "certain other crimes" and hang him if he did not; when he confessed, he was "immediately strung up."

None of the reports gives the exact date of the hanging, the number of vigilantes, or Smith's race. The dispatch was dated January 23, 1888, and said the news had "just reached" Macleod, while a list published at the end of the year placed the hanging on January 21.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

Every report found goes back to the single dispatch from Macleod, which papers cut to different lengths. The Alexandria Gazette carried a one-line version on January 24 among its "News of the Day," and the Omaha Bee ran it the next day under "Nosey Smith Lynched," dated January 24. Papers in Dakota, Oregon and Montana printed it within the week, and wire copies were found as late as early February in papers in Alabama, Maryland, Kansas, Pennsylvania, Indiana and Wyoming.

In Montana, the Helena Weekly Herald headed the medium version "Lynched by Vigilantes," and the Bozeman Weekly Chronicle printed the fullest text, with the convent, the priest and the forced confession, under "'Nosey' Smith No More." Neither Montana paper added local reporting, and the papers presented the hanging as "the fate" Smith had once fled, without criticism of the vigilantes. Shortened briefs, such as those in a Dakota "Crimes and Casualties" column and a Wyoming paper's "From Washington" column, reduced the charge to abusing "his daughter," and the Iola Register's copy garbled the ending so that Smith "met a posse." In December a Michigan paper's list of "Victims of Judge Lynch" included "'Nosey' Smith at Sun River, Montana" under January.

The dispatch says vigilantes seized and hanged Smith, with no lawful authority mentioned, for abusing his daughters and after demanding a confession to other crimes (A3, A8); the number of vigilantes is never given, and all reports go back to one secondhand dispatch from Macleod, N.W.T. (A2, A4).

Every report traces to one dispatch from Macleod, N.W.T., relaying 'news' that had 'just reached' there (A2, A3, A4, A8); the year-end list (A19) is derivative, and no Montana report from Sun River itself was found.

accounts.label: Macleod dispatch, short wire version
accounts.gist: News reached Macleod that vigilantes had hanged "Nosey" Smith at Sun River for shamefully abusing his (two) daughters.

accounts.label: Macleod dispatch, medium version
accounts.gist: Adds that Smith was well known locally and was said to have come to Macleod two years earlier to escape hanging for abusing his daughters; returning to gain possession of them, he 'met the noose'.

accounts.label: Macleod dispatch, full version (Bozeman Chronicle)
accounts.gist: Smith had claimed his daughters were held in a convent near Sun River against their will; he crossed into Montana, tried to take them and beat a priest; vigilantes held him in a building, promised release if he confessed other crimes, and hanged him when he did.

framing.detail: Most papers ran one or two sentences of the Macleod dispatch under headlines like 'Nosey Smith Lynched' or in news-of-the-day columns, giving the accusation as the reason for the hanging without comment.

Montana's Helena Weekly Herald headed it 'Lynched by Vigilantes'; the Bozeman Weekly Chronicle's 'Nosey Smith No More' carried the fullest text, describing the hanging as 'the fate that has now overtaken him'.
At year's end a Michigan paper listed him among the 'Victims of Judge Lynch' for January.

conflicts.note: Most copies date the Macleod dispatch Jan. 23; the Omaha Bee and the Snow Hill, Md., Democratic Messenger date it Jan. 24. The Alexandria Gazette printed the item on Jan. 24 (A1), which fits a Jan. 23 dispatch.
